_sources.nihOds: NIH Office of Dietary Supplements fact sheets (Iron, Folate, Vitamin C, Vitamin K, Magnesium, Zinc, Potassium, Vitamin A, Calcium, Vitamin B12, Vitamin D, Vitamin E), https://ods.od.nih.gov/factsheets/list-all/; reference intakes as listed in build_draft_batch.py (RDA for adult women)

clam.desc: Mollusks, clam, mixed species, cooked, moist heat
clam.offers: Cooked clams are an exceptional source of vitamin B12 (about 84 µg in 3 ounces, many times the 2.4 µg reference), with zinc, vitamin C and about 22 g of protein for 126 calories.
clam.how: Steam in their shells with garlic, wine or broth, or add shucked clams to chowder, pasta and rice dishes. Discard any that stay closed after cooking.
clam.cycle: Iron needs are higher for women aged 19 to 50 (18 mg a day, against 8 mg for men), partly because of menstrual blood loss (NIH ODS). Clams provide iron too (about 2.4 mg in this serving), in a form that is absorbed more readily than plant iron. No phase-specific claim is made.
clam.evidence: Nutrient amounts and reference intakes only (USDA FoodData Central, NIH ODS).
clam.name: Clam

mussel.desc: Mollusks, mussel, blue, cooked, moist heat
mussel.offers: Mussels are rich in vitamin B12 (about 20 µg in 3 ounces), iron (about 32% of the reference), zinc and protein (about 20 g), with some omega-3 fats.
mussel.how: Steam in a covered pot with garlic, wine or tomato until the shells open, then serve with the broth. Discard any that stay closed.
mussel.cycle: Iron needs are higher for women aged 19 to 50 (18 mg a day, against 8 mg for men), partly because of menstrual blood loss (NIH ODS). Three ounces of mussels supply about 5.7 mg. No phase-specific claim is made.
mussel.evidence: Nutrient amounts and reference intakes only (USDA FoodData Central, NIH ODS).
mussel.name: Mussel

oyster.desc: Mollusks, oyster, eastern, wild, cooked, moist heat
oyster.offers: Six cooked oysters give an exceptional amount of zinc (about 33 mg, over four times the reference), vitamin B12 and iron, for only about 43 calories.
oyster.how: Eat cooked: steam, bake or fry them, or add to stews. Raw oysters carry a food-safety risk (see the caution).
oyster.cycle: No cycle-phase claim is made for oysters. Their very high zinc content means a smaller portion is plenty.
oyster.evidence: Nutrient amounts and reference intakes only (USDA FoodData Central, NIH ODS).
oyster.reviewNote: Six oysters provide about 33 mg of zinc, over four times the reference intake in one serving. NIH ODS lists a tolerable upper intake for zinc, but that value has not been read this session: check it before publishing and consider a caution or a smaller serving.
oyster.name: Oyster

sardine.desc: Fish, sardine, Atlantic, canned in oil, drained solids with bone
sardine.state: canned in oil, drained, with bones
sardine.portion: 1 small can, drained (USDA: 1 can, 3.75 oz = 92 g)
sardine.offers: Canned sardines, eaten with their soft bones, are rich in calcium (about 35% of the reference in one small can), vitamin B12 and vitamin D, with about 0.9 g of omega-3 fats and 23 g of protein.
sardine.how: Mash on toast with lemon, toss into pasta or salads, or eat straight from the can with bread. The bones are soft and edible.
sardine.cycle: Calcium needs are 1,000 mg a day for women aged 19 to 50 (NIH ODS); sardines eaten with their bones are one of the few non-dairy foods that give a substantial amount. No phase-specific claim is made.
sardine.evidence: Nutrient amounts and reference intakes only (USDA FoodData Central, NIH ODS).
sardine.name: Sardine

anchovies.desc: Fish, anchovy, european, canned in oil, drained solids
anchovies.offers: Canned anchovies are an intensely salty, savoury fish. Five anchovies give about 5.8 g of protein and 0.4 g of omega-3 fats for only 42 calories.
anchovies.how: Melt into sauces, dressings and pasta, or use a few to season roasted vegetables and lamb. A little goes a long way.
anchovies.cycle: No cycle-phase claim is made for anchovies. They are mostly used for flavour, in small amounts.
anchovies.evidence: Nutrient amounts and reference intakes only (USDA FoodData Central, NIH ODS).
anchovies.reviewNote: Canned anchovies are very salty; sodium is not shown and no salt caution has a source yet.
anchovies.name: Anchovies

scallop.desc: Mollusks, scallop, (bay and sea), cooked, steamed
scallop.offers: Cooked scallops are a lean, sweet shellfish: 3 ounces give about 17 g of protein, vitamin B12 (76% of the reference) and zinc for only 94 calories.
scallop.how: Sear briefly in a hot pan until golden outside and just opaque inside, or steam or poach them.
scallop.cycle: No cycle-phase claim is made for scallops.
scallop.evidence: Nutrient amounts and reference intakes only (USDA FoodData Central, NIH ODS).
scallop.name: Scallop

trout.desc: Fish, trout, rainbow, farmed, cooked, dry heat
trout.offers: A cooked rainbow trout fillet is one of the richest foods in vitamin D (about 13.5 µg, 90% of the reference) and gives vitamin B12, vitamin E, about 17 g of protein and 0.6 g of omega-3 fats.
trout.how: Pan-fry, bake whole or in fillets with lemon and herbs, or poach. The skin crisps well.
trout.cycle: Few foods contain much vitamin D. The reference for women 19 to 50 is 15 µg a day (NIH ODS), and a trout fillet supplies about 90% of it. No phase-specific claim is made.
trout.evidence: Nutrient amounts and reference intakes only (USDA FoodData Central, NIH ODS).
trout.name: Trout

canned-salmon.desc: Fish, salmon, pink, canned, drained solids
canned-salmon.state: canned pink salmon, drained solids (with skin and bones)
canned-salmon.offers: Canned pink salmon, eaten with its soft bones, gives vitamin B12, vitamin D (about 82% of the reference), calcium (about 24%) and 0.9 g of omega-3 fats, with about 20 g of protein in 3 ounces.
canned-salmon.how: Flake into salads, sandwiches, fish cakes and pasta, or mix with yoghurt and herbs. The soft bones can be mashed in.
canned-salmon.cycle: Calcium needs are 1,000 mg a day, and vitamin D 15 µg a day, for women aged 19 to 50 (NIH ODS). Canned salmon with the bones supplies a good share of both. No phase-specific claim is made.
canned-salmon.evidence: Nutrient amounts and reference intakes only (USDA FoodData Central, NIH ODS).
canned-salmon.name: Canned salmon

canned-tuna.desc: Fish, tuna, light, canned in water, drained solids (Includes foods for USDA's Food Distribution Program)
canned-tuna.state: canned light tuna in water, drained
canned-tuna.offers: Canned light tuna in water is a lean, convenient protein: 3 ounces give about 16.5 g of protein and 90% of the vitamin B12 reference for 73 calories. It has far less omega-3 fat than oily fish.
canned-tuna.how: Mix with yoghurt or mayonnaise for sandwiches, toss into pasta and salads, or bake into fish cakes.
canned-tuna.cycle: No cycle-phase claim is made for tuna. FDA and EPA list canned light tuna as a "Best Choice" for mercury; albacore (white) tuna is a "Good Choice".
canned-tuna.evidence: Nutrient amounts and reference intakes only (USDA FoodData Central, NIH ODS).
canned-tuna.reviewNote: Light (skipjack) tuna, a "Best Choice" in FDA/EPA advice. Albacore (white) tuna is a different record and a "Good Choice".
canned-tuna.name: Canned tuna

haddock.offers: Cooked haddock is a lean, mild white fish: 3 ounces give about 17 g of protein, vitamin B12 (75% of the reference) and potassium for 77 calories.
haddock.how: Bake or poach in milk or stock, pan-fry, or use in fish pie and chowder.
haddock.cycle: No cycle-phase claim is made for haddock.
haddock.evidence: Nutrient amounts and reference intakes only (USDA FoodData Central, NIH ODS).
haddock.name: Haddock

pollock.desc: Fish, pollock, Atlantic, cooked, dry heat
pollock.offers: Cooked pollock is a lean, mild white fish with about 21 g of protein, vitamin B12 and magnesium (24% of the reference) in 3 ounces.
pollock.how: Bake, pan-fry or poach, or use in fish tacos and fish pie. It is the fish in many frozen fillets.
pollock.cycle: No cycle-phase claim is made for pollock.
pollock.evidence: Nutrient amounts and reference intakes only (USDA FoodData Central, NIH ODS).
pollock.name: Pollock

crab.desc: Crustaceans, crab, alaska king, cooked, moist heat
crab.offers: Cooked crab (Alaska king) is a lean shellfish with zinc (about 81% of the reference), vitamin B12, magnesium and about 16.5 g of protein in 3 ounces.
crab.how: Serve warm with lemon, fold into salads, cakes and pasta, or add to soups.
crab.cycle: No cycle-phase claim is made for crab. This record is Alaska king crab; other crab varies.
crab.evidence: Nutrient amounts and reference intakes only (USDA FoodData Central, NIH ODS).
crab.reviewNote: The catalogue entry "crab" is generic; the record is Alaska king crab.
crab.name: Crab

shrimp.desc: Crustaceans, shrimp, mixed species, cooked, moist heat (may contain additives to retain moisture)
shrimp.portion: 3 ounces cooked (USDA: 3 oz = 85 g), about 12 large
shrimp.offers: Cooked shrimp are a lean shellfish: 3 ounces give about 19 g of protein, vitamin B12, zinc and vitamin E for about 101 calories. The USDA record notes that shrimp may contain additives that retain moisture.
shrimp.how: Sauté, grill or steam briefly until just pink and firm, then add to stir-fries, pasta, salads and curries. They overcook quickly.
shrimp.cycle: No cycle-phase claim is made for shrimp.
shrimp.evidence: Nutrient amounts and reference intakes only (USDA FoodData Central, NIH ODS).
shrimp.name: Shrimp

sea-bass.desc: Fish, sea bass, mixed species, cooked, dry heat
sea-bass.offers: Cooked sea bass is a lean, mild fish with about 20 g of protein, magnesium and potassium in 3 ounces, and 0.65 g of omega-3 fats.
sea-bass.how: Bake, pan-sear skin-side down for crisp skin, or steam whole with ginger and spring onion.
sea-bass.cycle: No cycle-phase claim is made for sea bass. Which fish this means affects its mercury level (see the caution).
sea-bass.evidence: Nutrient amounts and reference intakes only (USDA FoodData Central, NIH ODS).
sea-bass.reviewNote: "Sea bass" is ambiguous. FDA/EPA lists black sea bass as a Best Choice and Chilean sea bass as a Good Choice (more mercury). The USDA record is "sea bass, mixed species". Decide which fish the catalogue means before publishing.
sea-bass.name: Sea bass

salmon.desc: Fish, salmon, Atlantic, farmed, cooked, dry heat
salmon.offers: Cooked farmed Atlantic salmon is a rich source of omega-3 fats (about 1.8 g in 3 ounces), vitamin D (about 74% of the reference) and vitamin B12, with about 19 g of protein.
salmon.how: Bake or roast with lemon and herbs, pan-sear skin-side down, or poach and flake into salads and pasta.
salmon.cycle: The reference intake of vitamin D for women aged 19 to 50 is 15 µg a day (NIH ODS), and few foods supply much; 3 ounces of salmon provides about three quarters of it. No phase-specific claim is made.
salmon.evidence: Nutrient amounts and reference intakes only (USDA FoodData Central, NIH ODS).
salmon.reviewNote: Farmed Atlantic salmon; wild salmon differs (less fat, less omega-3).
salmon.name: Salmon

cod.desc: Fish, cod, Atlantic, cooked, dry heat
cod.offers: Cooked cod is a lean, mild white fish with about 19 g of protein, vitamin B12 and magnesium in 3 ounces, and only 89 calories.
cod.how: Bake, poach or pan-fry, or use in fish and chips, stews and curries. It flakes easily, so handle gently.
cod.cycle: No cycle-phase claim is made for cod.
cod.evidence: Nutrient amounts and reference intakes only (USDA FoodData Central, NIH ODS).
cod.name: Cod

flounder.desc: Fish, flatfish (flounder and sole species), cooked, dry heat
flounder.offers: Cooked flounder and sole are delicate flatfish with about 13 g of protein, vitamin B12 and vitamin D (20% of the reference) in 3 ounces, for only 73 calories.
flounder.how: Pan-fry or bake briefly, or roll fillets around a filling. They cook in a few minutes.
flounder.cycle: No cycle-phase claim is made for flounder.
flounder.evidence: Nutrient amounts and reference intakes only (USDA FoodData Central, NIH ODS).
flounder.name: Flounder

halibut.desc: Fish, halibut, Atlantic and Pacific, cooked, dry heat
halibut.offers: Cooked halibut is a firm, mild white fish with about 19 g of protein, potassium (17% of the adequate intake), vitamin D (33% of the reference) and vitamin B12 in 3 ounces.
halibut.how: Bake, grill or pan-sear, or poach in a flavoured broth; its firm flesh holds together well.
halibut.cycle: No cycle-phase claim is made for halibut. FDA and EPA list it as a "Good Choice" for mercury (see the caution).
halibut.evidence: Nutrient amounts and reference intakes only (USDA FoodData Central, NIH ODS).
halibut.name: Halibut

mackerel.desc: Fish, mackerel, Atlantic, cooked, dry heat
mackerel.offers: Cooked Atlantic mackerel is a rich, oily fish: 3 ounces give vitamin B12 (many times the reference), magnesium (about 27%), potassium, about 20 g of protein and 1 g of omega-3 fats, for 223 calories.
mackerel.how: Grill, bake or pan-fry with lemon, or serve smoked in salads and on toast. Its strong flavour suits sharp, acidic partners.
mackerel.cycle: No cycle-phase claim is made for mackerel. FDA and EPA list Atlantic mackerel as a "Best Choice" for mercury, but not king mackerel.
mackerel.evidence: Nutrient amounts and reference intakes only (USDA FoodData Central, NIH ODS).
mackerel.reviewNote: The catalogue entry "mackerel" is generic; the record is Atlantic mackerel. A caution about king mackerel (a different, high-mercury fish) is added.
mackerel.name: Mackerel

red-snapper.desc: Fish, snapper, mixed species, cooked, dry heat
red-snapper.offers: Cooked snapper (the USDA record covers mixed species) is a lean, mildly sweet fish with about 22 g of protein, potassium (17% of the adequate intake), vitamin B12 and some magnesium in 3 ounces.
red-snapper.how: Bake or grill whole or in fillets with herbs and citrus, or pan-fry the fillets skin-side down.
red-snapper.cycle: No cycle-phase claim is made for snapper. FDA and EPA list snapper as a "Good Choice" for mercury (see the caution).
red-snapper.evidence: Nutrient amounts and reference intakes only (USDA FoodData Central, NIH ODS).
red-snapper.reviewNote: The record is snapper, mixed species, not specifically red snapper.
red-snapper.name: Snapper

tilapia.offers: Cooked tilapia is a very mild, lean white fish with about 23 g of protein, vitamin B12 and vitamin D (21% of the reference) in one fillet.
tilapia.how: Bake, pan-fry or grill, or use in tacos and stews. Its mild flavour takes well to spices and sauces.
tilapia.cycle: No cycle-phase claim is made for tilapia.
tilapia.evidence: Nutrient amounts and reference intakes only (USDA FoodData Central, NIH ODS).
tilapia.name: Tilapia
